newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Bankers urge caution as Vietnam mulls devaluation.
newsitem.headline: Bankers urge caution as Vietnam mulls devaluation.

text.p: As Vietnam prepared for a currency devaluation to tackle its growing balance of payments problem, bankers and economists warned on Monday that a sudden slide in the currency's value could cause as many problems as it solves.
Cao Si Kiem, governor of the central State Bank of Vietnam, was in Washington presenting plans for a devaluation of the local currency, the dong, to the World Bank and International Monetary Fund.
Before leaving, he dropped an oblique reference to the need for devaluation to bolster exports and put a brake on burgeoning imports.
But he gave no indication of the extent to which the dong, which has been steady at around 11,000 per dollar for several years now, would be devalued or over what period of time.

Bankers and economists say a cut in the value of the dong could help trim the country's trade gap, which stood at a record $3.25 billion in the first eight months of this year -- a near six-fold increase from the same period of 1995.

"If last year everyone was concerned about inflation and the year before about the fiscal deficit, this year what's emerging is some concern on the trade side," said one senior Western banker who declined to be named.
The communist country's reform-driven economic explosion has generated a hefty balance of payments deficit, which has this year crept above 10 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

"That's not something you can sustain over three or four years without some adjustment," the banker said. "One of the ways you adjust is to let the exchange rate take some of the pressure off the import burden."
Nevertheless, he and others cautioned against an unbridled dash to make imports more expensive and exports cheaper.
"My position is to go ahead very cautiously, step by step and not too hastily," said Le Dang Doanh, chairman of the Central Institute for Economic Management.

He said the dong should not be allowed to drift lower than 12,000 to the dollar, which would amount to a nine-percent devaluation. He said that, as a first step, the central bank should aim for a five-percent drop in the dong's value.
"I'm not a proponent of the massive devaluation," said David Hutcheson, Hong Kong Bank's top executive in Vietnam.
He said a dramatic devaluation could undermine public confidence in both the local currency and the banking system, which the central bank has been working hard to build up.
Many Vietnamese remain wary of banks, preferring to stash their savings -- often dollar bills or gold -- under the mattress at home.
Doanh also warned that a devaluation would raise the cost of importing capital goods, potentially stunting growth in domestic and foreign investment and, ultimately, exports.
The senior banker said the move would also make it more expensive for Vietnam to service its external debt, a large component of the fast-growing current account deficit.

Earlier this year, Hanoi reached a framework agreement on restructuring its approximately $1.0 billion debt to foreign commercial creditors. But foreign bankers say approval of the deal is unlikely to come before next year.
